achieved.quote: Among all randomized patients, final mean daily dose was 11.2 mg (among patients taking enalapril it was 16.6 mg).
achieved.notes: Titration (Kondo Table 1): 2.5 mg bid run-in 2-7 days, then 2.5 mg bid 1 wk or 5 mg bid, 5 mg bid 2 wk, 10 mg bid if 5 mg bid tolerated. Footnote: usual start 5 mg bid (10 mg/day), 2.5 mg bid if high risk; 5 mg/day used here as the lowest start. 16.6 mg is the enalapril arm; 11.2 mg is the blend of both arms (placebo arm up-titrated blind). At the final visit 49.3% of the enalapril group took 20 mg daily. Active run-in was used, so run-in intolerant patients are excluded. Sibling proxies use the lowest formulary-flagged target daily dose (Lisinopril 20, Ramipril 10, Captopril 150 mg/day); Lisinopril also has a flagged 40 mg target (see ATLAS). Independent cross-check from the primary-data reanalysis (Lam 2018, PMID 28980368): "the final mean daily dose of either study drug was 11 mg and at the final visit, 49% of patients in either treatment group were receiving target doses."

dose_comparisons.endpoint_notes: Crude mortality 15.5% placebo vs 6.0%, 6.7%, 1.1% with increasing carvedilol dose (P<.001 for trend); all three combined: 73% lower all-cause actuarial mortality. Hospitalization lower by 58% to 64% (P=.01). No per-dose HRs in the abstract. EF improved 5, 6, 8 units vs 2 with placebo (linear dose response). Mild-to-moderate HF, n=345, 6 months, so mortality counts are small; the 6.25 and 12.5 mg bid doses (12.5 and 25 mg/day) were each associated with benefit.

source.citation: Bristow MR et al. Circulation 1996;94:2807-16

dose_comparisons.quote: carvedilol was associated with dose-related improvements in LV function (by 5, 6, and 8 ejection fraction [EF] units in the low-, medium-, and high-dose carvedilol groups, respectively, compared with 2 EF units with placebo, P < .001 for linear dose response) and survival (respective crude mortality rates of 6.0%, 6.7%, and 1.1% with increasing doses of carvedilol compared with 15.5% in the placebo group, P < .001)

dose_comparisons.endpoint_notes: OBSERVATIONAL, not randomized, in patients selected as under-treated, with treatment-indication-bias correction. 22% reached the recommended ACEi/ARB dose and 12% the beta-blocker dose. Under 50% of recommended dose: higher risk of death and/or HF hospitalization vs 100%. 50-99%: comparable to 100% or more. Numeric HRs for the dose strata are not in the abstract (only HR 1.72, 1.43-2.01 for ACEi/ARB and 1.70, 1.36-2.05 for beta-blockers in patients not reaching dose because of symptoms, side effects or organ dysfunction). Sex analysis (Santema, Lancet 2019, PMID 31447116, abstract): in men lowest hazard at 100% of recommended dose; in women about 30% lower risk at 50% of the recommended doses with no further decrease above; 23-25% reached target ACEi/ARB, 13-14% beta-blocker. Women had lower weight (72 vs 85 kg).

dose_comparisons.quote: Patients reaching 50-99% of the recommended ACE-inhibitor/ARB and/or beta-blocker dose had comparable risk of death and/or heart failure hospitalization to those reaching ≥100%.

dose_comparisons.endpoint_notes: OBSERVATIONAL within a randomized trial (time-updated Cox, post hoc). Endpoint is the primary composite (CV death or HF hospitalization), not death or HF hospitalization separately. Sacubitril/valsartan vs enalapril HR after a dose reduction 0.80 (0.70-0.93); in patients with no dose reduction 0.79 (0.71-0.88). Any dose reduction predicted a higher subsequent event risk (HR 2.5, 2.2-2.7). This compares the two drugs at lower doses, NOT either drug against placebo or dose against dose; Kondo adds it held "whether the reduction was to 50%-100% of target or to <50% of target dose" (secondary).

dose_comparisons.quote: the treatment benefit of sacubitril/valsartan over enalapril following a dose reduction was similar (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.70-0.93, P < 0.001) to that observed in patients who had not experienced any dose reduction (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.71-0.88, P < 0.001).

dose_comparisons.endpoint_notes: Strategy trial in acute HF, open label, stopped early. Primary: HF readmission or all-cause death to day 180, 15.2% vs 23.3%, risk ratio 0.66 (0.50-0.86), adjusted risk difference 8.1% (2.9-13.2), P=0.0021. Death alone and HF readmission alone were NOT in the abstract. Fatal adverse events 25 (5%) vs 32 (6%). The comparison bundles dose, pace, monitoring and visit frequency, so the benefit is not attributable to dose alone. Post hoc within the high-intensity arm (Cotter, JAMA Cardiol 2024, PMID 38150260; observational, 515 patients): at 2 weeks 7.6% low (<50% of optimal), 49.3% medium (50-<90%), 43.1% high (>=90%) dose; each 10% increase in average percent optimal dose: aHR 0.89 (0.81-0.98) for HF readmission or death and 0.84 (0.73-0.95) for death.
